notes.title: The Start of the Festival of Murugan
body: Kanda Sashti (the Tamil colloquialisation of Skanda Sashti) is calculated according to the lunar tithi, specifically Shukla Sashti — the sixth tithi of the waxing fortnight (bright half) of the lunar month of Aippasi. The six-day observance begins with Shukla Pratipada directly following Deepavali Amavasya.

For us, it’s a breathless continuation of a series of rituals that began with Navaratri–before which, mercifully, there had been something of a break. It’s not for no reason that the period starting with Aadi is described as the Indian “festival season.” It’s less common to call it the season of samharams–but in essence, it really is that. Darkness descends, lengthily and brooding, fire light is the only thing that can shine through and must be made to do so, and after prolonged and intense battles–it does. Nearly every festival that happens in this season reiterates this essential idea.

Kanda Sashti or Sashti for short is the major festival of the Murugan temples we are following, though everyone with a Murugan presence in the temple will of course mark and honour it. The parayanam groups at Vedapuriswara for example, don’t switch their chanting to some other temple; they continue at Vedapuriswara but focus on Balamurugan specifically. We have decided, however, to manage the intensity of this period by focusing mostly on the two Murugan temples in our set of 15: the incredibly popular Ghousiga Balasubramania Swami temple, and the Siva Subramania Swami temple at Lawspet. There are other Murugan temples around: Saaram Murugan has a popular reputation, too, Muthialpet Murugan isn’t far behind. Of course, there is Mailam whose aadheenam has no small influence on local shrines. “Tell a story about just how many Murugan temples are in Pondicherry,” one Mudaliar man from the Lawspet temple, the ubhayakara for the Vaikasi Vishakam Satru Samhara Trishita Homam, once urged me. “There are no less than 12 here.” I’m not sure we’ll get to that, but his emphasis wasn’t lost on me.

Both Lawspet and Ghousiga started with Vigneswara pujas, which entail abhishekam for Vinayaka and the reigning deity, followed by a ganapati homam. There is also a vastu shanti (with its iconic setting alight and pulling of a straw vastu purusha figure around the temple and then out of it, to the ominous, repeated 3 measured beats of the tavil), and a mrtsangrahanam + ankurarpanam, or the collection of sacred mud and the sowing of sprouts as a symbol of growth and well-being.

Thanks to all sorts of practical considerations, not the least of which was learning to manage the physical distance between Ghousiga and Lawspet as we learned the Sashti ropes, so to speak, we couldn’t stay for the whole session of invocatory pujas at Lawspet. But it was clear that they were following every step with care, with no less than 5 priests around, including non-regulars called in to help. Ghousiga had no additional priests. Vinayaka (the main statue at the back left) got a quick abhishekam, while the utsava murti was already ready to go–a fact which seemed odd, given that the utsavars are usually readied at the same time as the main deities for the pujas ahead. So then there was a deeparadhanai, and He was moved to the position of officiating deity at the homam space, set up to the right of the main deity, with a makeshift yagasala prepared in the niche that doubles as a palliyarai, facing west. So the 9 Kalasas there faced west, Utsavar Ganesha too faced them and the East. There was no elaborate agni kundam, but an almost tiny clay pot used in lieu. The three priests we see there all the time (the older Gurukkal, his son, and another we learned is a relative) performed all the pujas. Since there is no stala vriska here or source of mud in this granite-floored temple, the purappadu had to begin–Vinayaka was taken clockwise around the block to the small turmeric-smeared stone near the bank that is now there–and the sacred earth collection happened there. It, too, was symbolic: the pavement is also granite-covered.

A lady who had seen me with my phone and camera struck up a conversation; this evening is her mother’s ubhayam. Dhanalakshmi-ammal, if I may call her that, had apparently started supporting the elder Ghouse with Rs 60 in the early days, for Murugan abhishekams and now sponsors 3 temple events on her own, managing to get the funds needed somehow (her daughter said): Varsha Pirappu (15 litre abhishekam for Murugan), 1st Saturday of Purattasi abhishekam for Perumal (who sits in the koshta right behind Murugan in the prakaram), and then these preparatory pujas at the start of Sashti (for Rs 40,000). “There used to be a tree here,” she told me of the place where the Mrtsangrahanam happened. But now it is all completely paved and the only sign of a former life is in the stone that remains to mark the puja spot.
So Vinayaka’s purappadu on mooshika vahana happens, and only then the invocatory pujas are completed, before He continues on his way.

notes.title: A Camera-Happy Temple
body: The flag went up at Ghousiga at 630am. We know that precisely because that’s when we got there, thinking it’s roughly when the pujas begin (the patrikai lists times which no temple accurately follows, and we’ve become decent at calculating for lateness, but sometimes just get it all wrong). So then there are Khadir-sir and the younger priest, tying the flag to the kodi maram. The Ghousiga temple has three entrances – one to the south, two facing east, with one of these directly in front of the moola murti. When the queues are long, the queueing lines  themselves block the south entrance, and people are guided to the east moola murti entrance. The third entrance is like a private one at this point, controlled from within. We thought we were stuck watching what we could from outside, which wasn’t very much at all. But then someone at the third entrance allowed us to come in, denying another man entry on the grounds that “they [as in we who were let inside] have cameras.”

Wow, I thought. First temple to grant us entry because we have cameras, not in spite of them. It made me think again about what this magical box we carry around with us, to “take” photos–it’s always regarded as taking; one man at Kannika a long time ago had said that, you take so many photos, implying that a few might have been ok, but a lot is a different matter–actually signifies. I’ll leave that musing for later, just noting for now that even in temples with rules stricter than Ghousiga, the photos signal attention–desired, in this socially mediated show-case friendly Instagrammable world. They put the Brahma into the brahmandam, dare I say.

Once inside, we got to see that all the dhvajarohanam rituals had been completed in the pretty small area to the left of the kodi maram, with people in queue allowed to stand on the other side of it. We walked in to the bali peethams being given their customary, preemptory, obligatory feedings. After this began the bhakta-driven part of the day, with people bringing flowers, archanai offerings, and specifically green (Pachai Mani Malai) and black beaded malas to be placed at the feet of the deity and then around their necks by the priests. Then the tying of the kaappu for several – men and women, those associated with this specific temple utsavam and not, it seemed. Then of course the purappadu, which becomes Ghousiga’s signature event because of the energy, vigour and dance of it all. One of the tavil players said later than his fingers were broken (they discussed salves) and that the dance was “over” (over the top) these 6 days, and would be about half this in the days after Sashti. The purappadu “route” is one circle in the inner prakaram, stopping at the main shrine for blessings, then out and to Thulasi Mariamman, and then the dance – and then down Bharati–Nehru–MG road all the way back to the railway station road. Apparently the day the chariot gets pulled, it goes all the way to Thyagaraja street, making the whole area within the boulevard effectively this temple’s maada veethi.

Interspersed with all the dance was the interaction with this swinging hanging angel that had a cup full of flowers and was swung in a way that would, eventually, release all the flowers at its apogee, onto Murugan himself (who was by the way looking very grand on the chandra prabhai, though he was almost sitting on the crescent moon rather than being framed by it). All phones were out to capture this – and handles like @yen_pondy acting like advertising agents for Ghousiga rather than the reporters they’re technically supposed to be (they barely ever post on Lawspet, for example, but Ghousiga got major previews many days ahead–clearly they were impressed). A bit gimmicky maybe, but certainly a crowd pleaser to see everyone’s beloved Murugan being so feted.

notes.title: Tracking Sashti on Pratipada (Muthal Naal) Across Three Temples
body: Vedapuriswara has Murugan in three forms: the moolavar at the back, with Valli-Devasena, the Balamurugan in front, and Palani Andavar facing west. In the Chetty temple, Murugan-Valli-Devasena are also in the same position at the back, except it’s Palani Andavar in front where the Balamurugan is at Vedapuriswara. Quite the switch! Both temples do the vel-vanguthal on Day 1 of Sashti, though we don’t make it to the Chetty event as we already have split ourselves between Ghousiga and Lawspet, with a slice of Nandhikeswara in between. Chetty Gurukkal chided us for that later: you could have called and found out the timings, he said.

Nandhikeswara does a 4pm abhishekam and alankaram – but this time not by re-creating Murugan’s face, instead using the thirumeni’s own face and building a surprisingly proportionate form, as is their speciality. Today’s Alankaram is inspired by Thiruparankundram Murugan’s Maharajalilasana, though our temple does not have the left hand form that rests on Murugan’s thigh, so they made it a varada mudra. I rushed there at 820pm, to find the priests closing shop. I got there just in time to take two photos and leave.

Back to Vedapuriswara. During Sashti, Balamurugan gets an abhishekam each morning, and the Moolavar gets one along with the utsavars in the afternoon. The morning session is accompanied by parayanam (same group that sings outside the Nayanmar mandapam), and Kanda Sashti Kavacham recitation in the evening.

Today is when the Sivan Koyil does the “vel vanguthal” – which means that Murugan gets the Vel or spear from his mother, who is in this case Tripurasundari. So around 730pm, there is a deeparadhanai at the alankara mandapam at the back, then Raja Ganapathi and others are there to carry the deities out. They circle and bring them to face Ambal. After the usual deeparadhanai, curtain closes, opens, Guru mama comes out, goes to the Murugan standing with flowers (everyone touches in participation), does a tiny puja there, curtain closes again, and when it opens there is Kalyana Sundara Gurukkal with a scarf on his head holding up a beautiful ruby-studded vel which he carries with uncommon seriousness and intention while Ayyappan swami faces him walking backwards, splashing chandanam (sandalwood) water like it must be holi in Pondicherry, and someone else throws rose petals. Vel goes to Gurumama, he places it (while I’m struggling to get any useful photos with the jostling crowd, incredibly poor lighting, and of course the chandanam that has now landed on my camera lens).

The energy of this moment is incredible though. Someone right behind me calling out “Vettrivel Muruganukku” – and the whole entire crowd answers, with equal vigour, “Harohara!” It always sounds like “arogara,” it’s loud, but it’s moving, it’s not like anything we’ve heard before. Murugan as Devasenapati commands it, I suppose. But he’s also the god of love, as much as he is of war, and he is the beautiful one (azhagar), and it’s hard not to be in awe.

On to Ghousiga. Murugan alankaram here is always both minimalist in colour and His postures grand–to match the reception he receives here. Pujas follow the usual steps, but everyone waits for the purappadu. Once Murugan is lifted onto the shoulders of the men who carry him for the evening, it’s dance-dance-dance. He responds to the priest’s prayers at the moolasthanam and at the yagasala, rounding and bouncing. When He emerges from the temple’s far right entrance, someone holds a green cloth and swirls it repeatedly. Green is a colour often associated with him–perhaps it’s the peacock, perhaps it’s the sense of his eternal youth and vigour. Then the temple’s men go through their usual motions. Khadir Sir always guides and leads–it’s his temple, after all. His son Farhaan is never far behind, often one of the men carrying. Murugan goes to Thulasi mariamman first – she throws flowers on him, he acknowledges with movement. The nadaswaram players start slow and lift the tempo as the men lift and move Murugan. “Ghousiga, Ghousiga!” is the repeated cry. At some moment, they pause for the angel – a little wooden figure who typically lives at the top of the exterior tin roof, and who operates by some pulley system to swing-swing-swing and eventually by the arc of its own motion, throw flowers on Murugan’s face. It’s a great charmer and crowd pleaser. This happens thrice. The dance continues a bit, Murugan retreats to his vahana. It takes long to set up there, but when he does, the purappadu begins.

I’m not sure how many follow Murugan after this, on his long and difficult route through some of the most crowded and messy of Pondicherry’s market areas. We sometimes catch him on the way. But once he leaves the temple, really the deity is on his own, accompanied only (but always) by Vinayaka, Veerabahu, one of the junior temple priests, the men operating Ghousiga’s trusty red tractor, and the nadaswaram-tavil players of course. And maybe for the Gods as it is for us in this life, those who stay with you after the crowds have gone are really the only ones who matter. And they are enough.

In his calculus of costings, the Draupadi Amman temple priest had once told us of the computations involved in designing their chariot–the weight determines who will be there to pull, and how much they’ll charge. “But people pull the chariot, don’t they?” I had asked. “On the way out, yes, for some time!” was the quick reply. “But who brings the Amman home?” Touche. Their paths are lonely ones, in the end.

notes.title: The Flag Goes Up on Sashti Muthal Naal
body: The ubhayakara sankalpam for the day began at 230pm, outside the Siva Siddhi Vinayaka shrine. The opening veneration to he who clears obstacles and enables new realisations did not just end with yesterday’s Vigneswara Puja. It is a pattern that repeats across all the different layers of the Mahotsavam. We observed it in the following abhishekam for Murugan, which only began after there was one for Vinayaka. The bathing of Murugan was a bathing of four – the moola stone deities, the utsava deities, the utsava murti of Siva Shanmukha and the protective astra murti. The abhishekam itself was modest, but the presence of the four Murugans together seemed to invoke an intense concentration of His energy – youthful and victorious.

This was followed by the preparation of the flag. It was our first time seeing the flag entirely unfurled, extending comfortably to be over 30ft. The entire stretch of cloth was twisted and rolled, leaving exposed only the very end which had the painting of the Spear, with the Peacock, the Rooster, and a few lamps.

The Navaveerargal shrine at the back was installed during the Kumbhabhishekam 10 years ago. And since then, this shrine’s responsibility during Kanda Sashti has been taken by a group primarily consisting of young men. (Later heard the priest refer to them as the “Veerabahus”, but need to find out more.) This group then proceeded with a very modest abhishekam for the Navaveerargal, all of whose utsava murtis were also brought out and placed in front of their respective moola murtis. The Veerabahu utsava murti is smaller because it existed even prior to the Kumbhabhisheka addition. These Navaveeras are children of the nine Shaktis who were born when nine stones scattered and fell from Parvati’s anklets. Apart from these Navaveeras, the Samhara Vel also is looked after by this group, which is part of the Navaveerargal abhishekam and stands at their centre.

Another hour passes by in preparation and alankaram. By 6pm all the utsavars are adorned and positioned outside the Vinayaka shrine to witness the dhvajarohanam, flag-hoisting. The dhvajastambha abhishekam begins first, with the thronging of devotees all around. The temple gateway is entirely flooded, with many like myself only getting glimpses of the scene from the gopuram stairway. Those unable to watch the dhvajastambha ceremony join the others who flock instead to the Shanmukha utsavar at the back. The lamp-tables are decked with beautiful sestet deepam formations honouring the six-headed one.

Meanwhile, after the dhvajastambha abhishekam, the priests all head to the yagasala, where the head-priest and his son are presented with honourary towels around their heads, and bring back the plate of kaappu sanctified kaappu threads. The flag is given one last pushparchanai, which is followed very interestingly by a small ceremony for the bheri, or thavil, or drum. The drummer too is honoured. The flag is finally raised and tied round the post.

The kaappu threads brought from the yagasala are then tied to Vinayaka, Murugan, Samhara Vel, Navaveerargal, Chandikeswara, the utsava murtis, Murugan’s peacock, [the balipeetham?], and finally to the dhvajastambha itself. Shodashopachara deeparadhanai is then done for the dhvajastambha and the utsava murtis, after which the utsava murtis are presented music by the thavil and nadaswaram players. The thavil players offer an intense jugalbandi. The bali peethams are fed after which the astra murti retreats back into the utsava mandapa.

All other utsavars are then raised on shoulders and taken to the yagasala for the “Veerabahu” kaappu, wherein “Veerabahu” referred to the group of men donning green veshtis and who take care of the Navaveera shrine. These men are all presented with yajnopaveethams, perhaps only for the duration of this festival, and were tied with kaappus. All deities were given one more aradhanai, and proceeded towards the entrance. We were all asked to step out of the temple to witness the Gopura Darshanam. The temple gates were closed and opened to the devotees’ chants of “Vettrivel Muruganukku Harohara”, revealing anew the deities in their grand procession for the night.

notes.title: Sashti Dwitiya or Sashti Irandaam-Naal
body: Dashed to Kamakshi Amman to find out the timings for the Rahu Ketu Peyarchi coming up, then to Ghousiga where again we had to come in through the side third door as the queues to the temple were long, long, long. We waited a long while for the curtain to open again, as the abhishekam was done and alankaram was going on inside. Alankaram also happening for the utsavar alongside – purappadu was supposed to happen at 8 or so, it was 1030 by the time that it seemed just about to begin. Rishabha vahana today, we noted this and did not stay for it.

But the time there was beautiful. The deeparadhanai was a little too quick to satisfy, but the younger priest chanting and singing more than amply made up for it. He repeated almost the whole sequence twice, for moolavar and for utsavar. It included a song, with this refrain: “Saravanabhava, Saravanabhava, Saravanabhava Pahimam–bhavasaravana, bhavasaravana, bhavasaravana Rakshamam.” I’ve a recording which I will try to transcribe and learn in the way I always did as a kid who found fun song recordings to learn.
This pattern of abhishekam, pujai and purappadu will repeat all the days of the festival.

We made it to the Chetty Koyil as one priest (who is new, haven’t seen him since the start, but he’s been a regular for some time now) was doing the abhishekam for Murugan at the back sannadhi, and another (also a regular now, new, we met him first at the Angalamman temple in town where he did a nice Kali abhishekam one evening) started the utsavar abhishekam in the alankara mandapam, next to the palliyarai in which the Ambal was seated alone and a gorgeous Bhikshatanar stood by her side.

Nandhikeswara in the evening: alankaram for Murugan was as he is at Pazhamudir Cholai. This made us ask if the plan was to have alankaram from all 6 of the Arupadaiveedu, but no. The last day would be Sikkal Singaravelan. But of course–his is the shakti that carries the vel to Thiruchendur.

notes.title: Sashti Mundraam Naal, or Sashti 3rd Day
body: Somewhere around 10am, we’re in Lawspet. The day’s pujas are just beginning, the Veerangal group is there–they’re charged with doing the abhishekam to the Navaveerargal or the 9 brave ones who together comprise the army led by Veerabahu in the battle against Soorapadman and his sons. The Vel makes its rounds of the temple, stopping at all major shrines and not forgetting the yagasala where there are pujas happening morning and evening kaalams (we try a few times to record the full yagasala puja, in vain because they start late or there’s too much noise, or far too many interruptions in the process. It never seems as central an aspect as many other elements of the vizha). Following this, the Vel and the Veerangal go out on procession, preceding Murugan of course, and accompanied by Vinayaka.

Close to 11am, Ghousiga–and they’re just finishing the morning prayers and getting ready for the purappadu. Murugan has a veena in his hands, the son of Veenadhara after all. Arunagirinathar’s Puya Vaguppu verse 17, from Tiruvaguppu gives us a description Murugan’s arms: they are musically accomplished, they know the characteristics of delightful ragas and play Kaisikai, Gowda, Varali, Dhanasi, Desi, Bhairavi, Kujjari and Panjuram on the veena–
இசைதனில் இனிய கயிசிகை கவுட வராளித
னாசி தேசி பயிரவி குச்சரி
பஞ்சு ரந்தெ ரிந்து வீணைக் கிசைந்தன
Source: Kaumaram, and listen to the recitation by Revathy Sankaran

In the evening, we stop by the Chetty Koyil for the puja and ul-purappadu. It’s as most else happens at the Chetty Koyil with these internal events: utsavars in the alankara mandapam, puja happens there, the deities are hoisted onto a vandi which is pushed around the temple thrice, stopping at the Sivan sannadhi on the first round.

Nandhikeswara Alankaram today: not temple associated, Raja alankaram, as though He is sitting in his durbar, they said. Likewise, apparently is Ghousiga’s alankaram, always more delicate in the use of colours and noteworthy also today because of the malas. Brown malas are usually vettiver, but here they are almonds, cardamom and cloves–scented, precious, beautiful, ingenious. And signs of the Indian tendency to want to shower lavishly and extravagantly on the body of the divine all the precious things the earth produces.

The man who goes by “pannisai_deva” on Instagram is here, clearly invited to sing for these sashti days. We see him a few times, and hear him sing this once. Today’s song is “ஆடு மயிலே! நிர்த்தம் ஆடுமயிலே!” from the Manjaippaattu by Sengalvaraya Pillai, recorded on Project Madurai. It’s a lovely, rhythmic song, on my list to learn:

ஆடு மயிலே! நிர்த்தம் ஆடுமயிலே! - தணிகை
ஆறமுக நாதன் வர ஆடு மயிலே!
பாடுமடி யார் பரவ ஆடு மயிலே! - சம்
பந்தன்வர என்றன் முனம் ஆடுமயிலே!

தணிகைமலைத்தேவன்வர ஆடுமயிலே! - தமிழ்
தத்திம் தித்திம் தத்திமென ஆடு மயிலே!
பணியுமெனைக் காத்துவர ஆடுமயிலே! - பரன்
பாலகுகன் ஏறிவர ஆடு மயிலே!

நீல மயிலே! மந்த்ர ரூப மயிலே! - நிதம்
நித்தன் அத்தன் ஏறிவரு சித்ர மயிலே!
கோல மயிலே! நீயே ஓல மயிலே! - அண்ட
கூடமுழு தோடினவி சேட மயிலே!

துங்க மயிலே! நாகபந்த மயிலே! - சிகைச்
சூட்டு மயிலே கவலை யோட்டு மயிலே!
வெங்கண் மயிலே! கந்தர் தங்கு மயிலே! - அன்பன்
வெற்றி பெற வந்துதவு கொற்ற மயிலே!

நேச மயிலே! அரன் பூசை உமையே - திகழ்
நின்னுருவங் கொண்டு செய்தாள் முன்னம் மயிலே!
ஆசை மயிலே! எங்கள் அருணகிரியாம் - அன்பர்
அன்றழைக்க வந்து நின்றாய் ஆதிமயிலே!

வாகை மயிலே! மணி நாக மயிலே! - மலை
மாதுதரு நாதனமர் சோதி மயிலே!
தோகை மயிலே! தருமோக மயிலே! - சுகச்
சுத்த நிலை இன்னதெனச் சொல்லு மயிலே!

தேவாதி தேவ னென் றாடு மயிலே - திருச்
செங்கொட்டு வேலனென் றாடு மயிலே!
சாவாப்ர சாதந்தந் தாடு மயிலே! - தனத்
தந்தான தானவென் றாடு மயிலே!

வேலா விசாக என்றாடு மயிலே! - மலை
வேந்தா குமார என்றாடு மயிலே!
பாலா விநோத என்றாடு மயிலே! - மலர்ப்
பாதா குகேச என்றாடு மயிலே!

தத்திமென நிர்த்தமிடு பச்சை மயிலே! - குக
சண்முகனை என்முன் வரப்பண்ணு மயிலே!
சத்திமயில் வஜ்ர மயில் சண்ட மயிலே! - தனித்
தங்க மயில் துங்க மயில் எங்கள் மயிலே!

செம்பொன் மயிலே! சித்ரபைம்பொன் மயிலே! - திருச்
செந்தின் மயிலே! பரங் குன்றின் மயிலே!
அம்பொன் மயிலே! எங்கள் நம்பன் மயிலே! - பணி
அஞ்சு மயிலே! நீயே தஞ்ச மயிலே!

வள்ளி மணவாள என்றே ஆடு மயிலே! - வான
மங்கை பங்க துங்க என்றே ஆடு மயிலே!
கொள்ளுநல மின்னதெனக் காட்டு மயிலே! - கோழிக்
கொடிக்கரத்துத் தேவனருள் கூட்டு மயிலே!

ஆறு திருப்பதியானென் றாடு மயிலே! - மெய்
யன்பருக்குக் கதியானென் றாடு மயிலே!
வேறுகதி யில்லை யென்றே ஆடு மயிலே! - எங்கள்
வேல வேல வேல என்றே ஆடுமயிலே.

அந்த மயிலே! ஆநந்த மயிலே! - சச்சி
தானந்தன் பாட நடம் ஆடு மயிலே!
சந்த மயிலே! எங்கள் கந்தர் மயிலே! - பிர
சண்ட மயிலே! சிகைக் கொண்டை மயிலே!

வாசுகி எடுத்துதறு வண்ண மயிலே! - தெய்வ
வள்ளிமலை நாதன்வரப் பண்ணு மயிலே!
ஆசுகவி பாடியுனை ஓதமயிலே! - வரம்
ஆதரித்துத் தந்தருளு நீதி மயிலே!

கோடி நமஸ் காரமுனக் காடு மயிலே! - கோடிக்
கோடிநமஸ் காரமுனக் காடு மயிலே!
பாடியுனைப் போற்றுகின்றேன் ஆடு மயிலே! - ஆடிப்
பாடிப் பாடிப்போற்றுகின்றேன் ஆடு மயிலே!

எப்போதும் போற்றி செய்வேன் எங்கள் மயிலே! - என்னை
ஏமனிடங் காட்டாதே எங்கள் மயிலே!
முப்போதும் பூஜை செய்வேன் எங்கள் மயிலே! - திரு
முருகனருள் கூட்டிவைப்பாய் எங்கள் மயிலே!

O peacock, dance! O peacock, perform your dance!
Dance as the six-faced Lord of Thanikai arrives!
Dance as the devotees sing and praise him!
Dance before me as Sambandan comes!

Dance as the Lord of Thanikai Hill arrives!
Dance to the rhythm: thathim, thithim, thathim!
Dance as the Lord comes to protect me, who bows to him!
Dance as Bala Guha, the Supreme Lord's child, mounts you!

O blue peacock! O peacock who embodies the mantra!
O beautiful peacock, dance as the Eternal Father mounts you!
O graceful peacock! You are the peacock whose call resounds!
O peacock who ranges throughout all the cosmic worlds!

O exalted peacock! O peacock adorned with serpent-like patterns!
O crested peacock, drive away my worries!
O fierce-eyed peacock, the one on whom Skanda resides!
O victorious peacock, come and help your devotee triumph!

O loving peacock! Long ago, Uma, the consort of Hara,
took your very form and brought you into being!
O beloved peacock! When our devotee Arunagiri called you,
you came and stood before him, O primordial peacock!

O victorious peacock! O jewel-like, serpent-adorned peacock!
O radiant peacock, the one on whom the Lord of the Mountain's Daughter rides!
O plumed peacock! O enchanting peacock!
Tell me, peacock, what that blissful, pure state truly is!

Dance, proclaiming him the God above all gods!
Dance, proclaiming him the Lord with the Vel of Tiruchengode!
Dance, granting the deathless prasada!
Dance to the rhythm of the syllables: thanath thaana thaana!

Dance, proclaiming him as Vela and Visakha!
Dance, proclaiming him as the King of the Mountain and Kumara!
Dance, proclaiming him as Bala and Vinoda!
Dance, proclaiming him as the Lotus-Footed One and Guhesa!

O green peacock, dance the rhythmic dance to the beat of thathim!
Bring Shanmukha, Guha, before my very eyes!
O peacock of Shakti! O diamond-like peacock! O mighty warrior peacock!
O unique golden peacock, O exalted peacock, our very own peacock!

O golden peacock! O peacock of radiant, fine gold!
O peacock of Tiruchendur! O peacock of Tirupparankunram!
O beautiful golden peacock! O peacock of our beloved Lord!
O peacock before whom all bow, you alone are our refuge!

Dance, proclaiming him the bridegroom of Valli!
Dance, proclaiming him the exalted Lord who shares the heavens with the Divine Maiden!
Show me what is truly worthy of being sought!
Unite me with the grace of the Lord who bears the rooster banner!

Dance, proclaiming him the Lord of the six sacred abodes!
Dance, proclaiming him the refuge of his true devotees!
Dance, declaring that there is no other refuge!
Dance, singing again and again: Vel! Vel! Vel!

O beautiful peacock! O blissful peacock!
Dance as Saccidananda sings!
O rhythmic peacock! O peacock of our Skanda!
O mighty peacock, with your crest gathered into a tuft!

O peacock of the hue of Vasuki!
Bring the divine Lord of Valli of the Mountain here!
O peacock, I sing spontaneous verses and recite your praises!
O righteous peacock, graciously grant and uphold the boon!

I offer you a crore salutations, O peacock!
I offer you tens of millions of salutations, O peacock!
I sing and praise you; dance, O peacock!
I dance, sing, and praise you again and again; dance, O peacock!

I shall always praise you, our peacock!
Do not consign me to Yama, our peacock!
I shall worship you three times each day, our peacock!
Unite me with the grace of Lord Murugan, our peacock!

notes.title: May the Battles Begin!
body: Yanaimukha Samharam at Lawspet. Our morning begins at the Yaga Sala where a new Veerabahu member, perhaps coming from afar and unable to join from day one, gets his yajnopavitam and kaappu. He then joins his brothers outside the Navaveerargal shrine from where they proceed on their routine Vel procession. Not needing to document this recurring procession once more, we drift towards the purappadu-ready deities sitting outside their alankara mandapam. The deities are the same processional ones – Vinayaka, Veerabahu and his brothers, and Murugan with Valli-Devasena. Also tentatively part of the formation is the astra murti no taller than a foot. Its Murugan is no taller than half a foot, and his two consorts are at most one-third. This astra murti only oversees the twice-daily bali offering. We also observe the serpentine form that adorns Vinayaka’s arching thiruvachi – two serpentine bodies beginning from either ends of the arch, joined by a single serpent head above and behind Vinayaka’s. We are uncertain whether it is indeed a serpent or mere adornment that suggests and invokes that resemblance – both of which find resonance with our earlier exploration of the Pavitrotsavam. The procession deities are soon lifted, taken around the prakara, venerated at the Yaga Sala where the concluding purnahuti is performed, and are brought out with a Gopura Darshanam to face Yanaimukhasooran who waits tall outside. The sooran is elephant-headed with four tusks capped with golden embellishments, and with four arms wielding only weapons: a mace, an axe, a sword and a shield. His torso is decked in jewels, and his trunk and forehead sport the Tripundram.

As Murugan, the Navaveerargal and the Samhara Vel take their places braving the sooran, a distant drumming is heard from behind that large body. Looking ahead we see a small troop consisting of 3 drummers, a few helpers, and two figures dressed and crowned in black with faces painted pink and red respectively. “They are the actors of the soorans”, we were told yesterday by Siva of the Veerabahu group. He also told us that the enactment of the Samharam has always been done by the Senguntha Mudaliars, whose origin traces back to the Navaveerargal. The soorans also were played by hereditary families of this sect, so much so that they were referred not by name but by ‘sooranveedu kaaran’ or ‘of the sooran house’. “But they have been unable to sustain it, so we have had to train actors from outside for this”, continues Siva. Very much like the soorans of Vallala Kottai at Angalamman and Mahisharooran of Nagamutthu Amman, they are dressed in black skirts and large black rooster-feathered crowns, with shirts and pants as close to black as possible. They are decked with thick heavy jewellery-like embellishments that are studded with mirrors, both on their chests and their shoulders, with the latter resembling small wings.

They march forward, past Yanaimukhasooran, past the Veerabahus, past the Samhara Vel, past Murugan, and straight into the temple to pray to Vinayaka. The sight is a living expression of the divine Leela. The Soorans are the opposing principles who, by seeking Vinayaka’s blessings, acknowledge their necessary role in the play to be divinely guided and ordained. This is followed by a brief swirling dance around the temple prakara, before heading out and taking their place at the feet of the Sooran murti. Perhaps it is fair to say that the pink-faced sooran represents Yanaimukhasooran who was iconographically present in the murti as well, and the red-faced sooran represented Soorapadman, eldest of the brothers and from whom they all draw their strength and pride. A kalasa is brought out presumably from the Yaga Sala and kept before the Sooran-triplet. A final few archanais aradhanais are offered to this kalasam, the water from which is then sprinkled over the soorans and the people. It would be revealing to know what deity is invoked into this kalasam that blesses the soorans. The procession then departs on its hour-long pradakshina through the Mudaliar streets after which it arrives at the Lawspet Main Road for the final showdown.

Murugan, the Navaveerargal and the Samhara Vel take their place by the Vinayaka temple on the middle of the road, and Yanaimukhasooran opposite to them some 70 meters away. So the battle begins. The Veerabahu members wielding vels and bows & arrows play the Navaveeras, and the lone pink-faced sooran plays Yanaimukhasooran wielding a comically little sword. There ensues a long animated verbal back and forth with both groups pressing ahead and retreating with the undulating dynamics at play. The dialogue tries to follow a script, but a spontaneous light-hearted chaos comes over and the sooran’s comical pokes and jibes send ripples of laughter among the watching crowd. The Veerabahus too cannot help but smile in the midst of their battle. They go back and forth multiple times, with a few particularly dramatic pushes from the sooran, answering which the Samhara Vel dramatically presses forward and blows some vibhuti upon the possibly wounded Veerabahus.

Finally, upon the Veerabahus’ dire need for help, Murugan rolls forward and in a very fleeting moment slays Yanaimukhasooran and returns. The brief moment is made to feel very charged and potent by all the movement and clamour around it. A cloth quickly wraps the yanai mukham signalling his Samharam, and a Vel abhishekam immediately begins back at the Murugan-end of the road-stage to pacify the charged Spear. The Veerabahus take turns to pour the milk, and this concludes the first of the three Samharams.
Nandhikeswara alankaram today: He’s with a veena, once again. See yesterday’s field note for more on this.

Ghousiga has its Samharam at night. We got there a little past 8, and in usual Ghousiga fashion there was a grand reception for Murugan inside the temple. The crowd is already beginning to grow in anticipation of the final Soorasamharam day, and entry into the temple during the festival hours is restricted. We have already seen the rounds of blessings and singings and dancings from inside, so we stay out this time. After his final dance in front of the makeshift Yaga Sala, Murugan steps down and out of the temple, though still kept from view by a temporary foldable gate that acts as a thirai. The often enormous crown/giridam of flowers resting on Murugan’s head peeks out above this gate, and one can see it steadily swaying awaiting the grand opening. The kudai is raised behind Him, and the gate swings open with a rapid crescendo of the thavil and nadaswaram.

A brief visit to the Thulasi Mariamman shrine is followed once again with dance-dance-dance of the deity and swing-swing-swing of the flower-tossing angel. This goes on for well over half-an-hour and at around 9pm Murugan emerges out to the road where Gajamukhasooran has been waiting all day. Just as we think we are about to see the Samharam, Murugan pivots the other way and marches on leaving the sooran confused and behind! Turns out that Murugan walks around through Latouche street and comes back to the Morisson street side of the temple to climb his vahana – today the silver Adhikara Nandi. Meanwhile, Gajamukhasooran is also wheeled onto Morisson street and aligned to brave Murugan. It is interesting to note that Vinayaka and Veerabahu, who are otherwise present for every purappadu, were not here today. Perhaps due to a lack of space since Adhikara Nandi vahana was entirely on shoulders? There was a brief pause after these to bring out the Vel. We could not see inside the temple due to the crowds, but horns and drums of the Kailaya Vadyam were certainly declaring some significant movement within. Soon the Vel emerged with its head sailing over peoples’. It was held by the elderly priest who seemed to have lost consciousness at the touch of the Spear, supported by Khadir Sir who held the priest with one hand and the Vel with the other. They went first to Gajamukhasooran, then into the hand of Murugan. A curtain was raised over the entire scene, and dropped, revealing a deeparadhanai – and so the Samharam began. The young priest Rajesh lead the way with the deepam of the archanai-thattu raised, and Khadir Sir and the elderly priest followed again with the Vel – the priest seeming in more agony at the touch of the Spear. They marched ahead nonetheless, and again as with Lawspet, one brief moment was all it took for Murugan to slay the sooran over whose face cloth instantly fell. The charged Vel was immediately brought back to the feet of Murugan where an abhishekam followed. It was touching to see Khadir Sir and his son Farhaan hold the Vel during this pacifying bath–now their claimed lineage and their tradition.

Deepa’s old friend and colleague from UT-Arlington, Ritu Khanduri’s daughter Vidula was in town and pulled along for both today’s rides. She got a real taste of what big tamasha temple vizhas can be like! But as a daughter of an anthropologist, she’s already been in the thick of things and is a dyed-in-wool pro!

notes.title: Pooradam Nakshatram
body: Viswaksena Varuda Thirunakshatra Saattrumurai Utsavam at Perumal Koyil. The Vishwaksena shrine is inside the ul-prakara of the temple which goes around the garbhagriha, and we were told that only the ubhayakaras would be allowed in to watch it. So we went only at noon to catch Perumal’s purappadu around this prakaram on his way to meet Vishwaksena. Watching Perumal pass through this stone-pillared prakaram invoked a sense of the old and ancient, for this is how it must have been in the earliest days of the temple when it was only as large as the structure around the sanctum, and the now ul-prakaram been its only prakaram. The light flowing down the sanctum’s Vimana’s side and seeping into this prakaram was soft and gentle despite the mid-day’s shadowless hour. Through it Perumal moved slowly, and rounding three corners, reached Vishwaksena on the north. The proceedings there were simple: a tulasi archanai for Perumal, followed by naivedyam and deeparadhanai for both, concluding with shadari and teertham for bhaktas. All were asked to then sit outside for Prasadam at which point we took our leave for Lawspet.

notes.title: The Battle Continues and Murugan Gets the Vel
body: Crowds are slowly gathering as the festival tends towards Sashti. Though the day proceeds through some now familiar motions – abhishekam for moolavar and utsavars in temple, abhishekam for the Navaveerangal, the vel’s pradakshinam, the movement of the decorated utsava murtis outside to be seated on the vahanas, their procession through the madaveethi with so many houses alive and ready to meet them enroute. They arrive on the main road near the small vinayaka shrine that was perhaps once on the side of the road, but now finds itself in the middle. No matter, one side of the road is set up with keeth roofing at two ends – the Sooran Kottai as it’s called on one end, and the place near the temple for Murugan and the Veerangal on the other.

I walk and talk with Siva enroute. He makes many interesting observations about how their group has built this temple’s traditions, or kept them going at any rate, starting from the time of the last Kumbhabhishekam in 2018. Prior to that, there was only Veerabahu as an utsavar, no moola murtis, and none of the other utsavar figures. Now their group of about 15, all of them from the area, many working elsewhere, return every year for this festival – they take care of navaveerangal abhishekam twice daily, and all matters involving the purappadu as well as the ritual enactments that happen. Siva doesn’t speak of a continuous lineage easily handed down, but one which they have had to wrest and claim as their own. Parents had other priorities, financial futures to secure (his family has a shop in the big market just inside the entrance across from Singapore steel, he said, 4th one as you enter) and so many “restrictions,” not the “liberations” that they could then bestow on the next generation. Generational transfer, as it turns out, may in these ways skip a generation. Not all elders were secure about handing over their traditional vocations to a younger group they feared may take with them their own livelihoods. The family that used to enact the asuras roles had no takers. So they had to hire and train new actors, ensuring new lineages and new commitments. I asked about the script they were following, how that has transferred from oral to written tradition–he spoke of it as an accrual of material from multiple sources, painstakingly written down and now practiced, enacted. Still more songs need to be recorded, he said. And it occurred to me then that a lot of us are doing this work of defragmentation – collecting the potshards from cupboards and dumps as it were, piecing them together, bringing them back to life.

Siva spoke also of murungai maram because there are many enroute and how you could tell a Mudaliar neighbourhood by the number of murungai trees in the area – it is the source of endless variety (poriyal, saar, koottu, more) from a single tree. These were trees so abundant nobody needed to buy from the market. Now, that’s different, and many of us do.

Today’s battle is with three of Soorapadman’s sons: Banugopan, Vajrabahu, and Agnimukha. Both Banugopan and Agnimukha are sons by Padmakomalai, herself the daughter of the asura architect Maya (and therefore Mayai herself), and associated with the fiery aspects of the sun: Banu+Kopan; the name is associated with an episode from his childhood in which he challenged the Sun, having been given Suryan as a plaything. Vajrabahu’s antecedents are less immediately clear (they may be part of this temple’s own retelling of Tamil Kanda Purana episodes), but he and Veerabahu make mutually challenging vows: the victor will make a ladder of the spine of Him whom he defeats, and climb it to sing the praises of Murugan (or Soorapadman, but we know it will be Murugan).

Once Banugopan and Vajrabahu are defeated, Agnimukha performs a homam to invoke Kali, who is conjured and arrives–but sees her own son Murugan in the battle and refuses to act opposite to him. This is all ritually recreated with fire on the streets. We wonder at some point why the parai-vadyakaras (men with the parai drums) disappear, but they reappear at the other end of the street with a blue, 10-armed, hair flying Kali figure. It’s time now for pyrotechnics. Kali dances in fire. She blows it, she is encircled by it, she emerges from it, she creates it, she eats it. Move, her hands gesture with surprising gentleness, when the fire lit from poured kerosene threatens to come our way. She’s given a poosani – ashgourd, on which she steps and into which she thrusts her trident (the ashgourd is often used like limes, to ward of dhristi, perhaps owing to its head-like form). She is given a bowl of red liquid; she drinks, she spits, she spews. Slowly she moves towards Murugan, carrying a clay neruppu vessel as the Thirunangais do during the Angalamman Mayana Kollai event. And once she sees her son there, She retreats and disappears.

All this sounds very dramatic and fearsome, but the 9 veerangal going up and down with their paper scripts, speaking to the caricatured Sooran character (all the ill-fated brothers played by a single man, who can be found locally if you ask for “sooran veedu” or Sooran’s house in the neighbourhood) – all this is quite comical, as is some of the dialogue shooting back and forth. I’m tired, says the Sooran, I’m hungry, let’s finish this fast, what are you a small child threatening someone like me? The call-and-repeat patterns of dramatic conversation make for amusing listening. Entertainment, after all.

Each day after the day’s asura quota has been vanquished (acted by the group of braves coming forward with the Vel, backed by Murugan and the Sooran’s head covered with a cloth), the Vel receives a cooling abhishekam, aradhanai, and the procession returns to the temple.
In the evening, is the Vel Vanguthal
Or, when Murugan receives the spear from his mother, Parvati, Parashakti.

In this telling of the Skanda story, Gajamukha is Tarakasura, brother to Simhamukha and Soorapadman who is the oldest and must be vanquished. Kashyapa and Maya unite in the form of elephants, simhas, goats (producing the daughter who is Ajamukhi). The first, handsome without equal, was Soorapadman. 3-2-1, goes the tale, so Tarakasura goes first, then Simhamukha, then Soorapadman himself. Ajamukhi makes cameo appearance as the goat that Murugan rides – this evening, as it turns out, after the vel vanguthal.

We heard a great deal about Sikkal from many who were around: சிக்கலில் வேல் வாங்கி, திருச்செந்தூரில் சம்ஹாரம்/ Sikkalil Vel vaangi, Tiruchenduril Samharam/ "Receiving the Vel at Sikkal, and performing the Samharam at Tiruchendur." The recreation of these events in Pondicherry then places us in this lineage of Sikkal and Thiruchendur.

Now, during the Vel Vaangum Utsavam, immediately after receiving the Vel, the bronze utsava murti of Singaravelar is said to develop beads of perspiration on face and body. The sweat is wiped off, but devotees report that it reappears. The phenomenon is traditionally understood as an expression of Murugan's Veeravesham – his intense warrior disposition as he prepares to go into battle against Soorapadman.

But this gives rise to what can only be described as competitive sweating. The Times of India’s Samayam in 2019 reported the Ghousiga murti sweating. Another report in 2024 reported the Saram Murugan sweating. I guess these reports do their rounds, as temples vie for trending miracles and crowd draws.

Lawspet Murugan seems (as of now) free of perspiration. The yagasala puja seems to happen in fits and starts. We try to record it, but then a dance (with an invited Malayalee group) begins, and the sound is much too loud to make any recording worthwhile. Screens are set up all around, showing the temple in situ. Soon, there is a crowd in the temple so dense it’s hard to believe there are that many who live in the area. The lights go out at one point, and the whole area is lit only by the lamplight from Parvati’s garbhagriha. It’s surreal but it doesn’t last as people quickly whip out phones and the lights come back on. A “corridor” from the Parvati shrine (she’s done up with chandana kaappu) to the end of the temple prakaram is clear, with the area at the top of the 3 stairs reserved for the nadaswaram and tavil players who do a concert at the Priest Sriram Gurukkal’s direction. He specifies ragas, they play–in a manner similar to performances at the dhvajarohana. He announces recitations of the veda, and the scholars present chant. A woman goes into some sort of trance, and it’s regarded as entirely normal for that to have happened. All this happens after a maha deeparadhanai, which is a spectacle to behold.

Our Navaveerangal group are holding up Murugan, in a standing alankara position, the floral prabhai behind him larger than usual. Siva has the Sengol. The spear is held by the same elderly man who keeps it all through. The elder priest and younger, the Gurukkal and his son, get the parivattam. Men are made to stand with baskets of flower petals as the elder priest moves to get the vel, and when he does, he is supported by his son. It is a moment of intense drama. Flower petals fly, the vel shakes, the priests must control it but they can only barely, and it is in limbo until it comes into Murugan’s waiting hands. The exhausted priest is carried away–he will be mobbed later for the vibhuti he will have in his hands, from the moolasthanam

Meanwhile Murugan, vel in hand, comes to the yagasala and then proceeds to move out for the evening’s purappadu – on a vahana that is the goat, representing (presumably the control of) the only child of the handsome Sooran not yet slain, his daughter Ajamukhi.
Nandhikeswara: we didn’t make it here today, and have the photos included here courtesy of Dewan Kandappa.

notes.title: The Greatest Battle of Them All: Soora Samharam
body: Many temples mark today in some form. Angalamman Koyil does a Murugan Abhishekam and maha deeparadhanai in the morning. Vedapuriswara, anticipating this day, does a 7am-5pm 36-time recitation of the Kanda Sashti Kavacham, on top of the daily 7am Balamurugan abhishekam, and later Murugan abhishekam, evening parayanam. We saw the arrangements made outside the Chetty Koyil for the samharam, and the bells still ringing at 11pm as we passed by en route to Ghousiga, but we have no images of these events.

Our morning was spent watching the procession at Lawspet and the raising of the kodi that was the spine of Vajrabahu, on which the Navaveerangal would climb later in the evening to sing songs of Murugan, Siva, and Amman (Parashakti). For being the gigantic spine of an asura, this structure was treated with significant reverences. Turmeric was applied, vibhuti and kunkumam, flowers. A small bell at the head represented Vajrabahu’s skull. Flowers. I was told to be careful not to step on the ropes that would be used by the waiting crane to haul this into position. This sort of reverence had either got to be purification –or acknowledgement of Vajrabahu’s having now become one with Murugan. A smaller wooden piece was first placed in a waiting hole in the road (the hole must always be there, just closed up the rest of the year and opened again for the festival) – the hole was anointed of course, by Sriram Gurukkal, with turmeric water, milk, chandanam and the like. Then the short pole placed and the hole packed with soil. The men all seemed to have a mighty good time doing all this. The crane then picked up Vajrabahu’s spine and it was carefully and painstakingly tied with many yards of thick rope to the wooden piece in the ground. A umikkal was additionally fixed at the back end for additional weight, and that was that.

Lawspet’s patrikai promised that Sooran would be “chased from world to world” and he perhaps was until coming to the final battleground, though the chasing happened only on the koyil’s maada veethi, celebrated by the pump-powered showering of enormous amounts of confetti. The crowd was now thick. Dancers and fire blowers performed on one end; this was pure entertainment. At the other end, women from the area had prepared maavu vilakku (millet, rice, honey–make a mix, anoint with turmeric and kunkuma, create an indent, fill with oil and light a wick) along with customary archanai thattu offerings and assembled these at the kodi’s base. The brave ones prayed (deeparadhanai), circled with the lamp, singing as they did, and then climbed the pole on the other end. It looked a little precarious at times, but Siva and one other went to the top, older men stayed on lower rungs. Once the brave ones were done singing, a small deeparadhana happened at the very top–and they descended. Since Lawspet is the only temple we know of that does this part of the event, it was our highlight. But now it was time for the Samharam.

In principle, this followed the storytelling and back-forth movements of the prior two days. Veeras threaten, Sooran threatens and challenges right back, and up and down until finally Murugan comes himself finishes him. In practice, however, this was a whole different scene because there was barely any standing room. Even the ritual performers had barely any room to put on their show. But we knew what would happen, this by now was almost anti-climax.

We found the climax at Ghousiga, reaching just as the samharam was happening, but not being able to see any of it because the whole road was jam-packed. People on walls, old vehicles on the sides, just whatever could give height. Murugan’s vel would have travelled to the waiting Soorapadman, and then his face would have been covered. As soon as this happened, the crowd started to dissipate. We could then move closer to see the vel abhishekam being done. Veerabahu was on a small horse facing Murugan, Vinayaka was on a similar vahana but beside him. A large group of drummers were having the time of their lives in the middle. Janardhanan came and joined midway, but Sivavijay’s wife from Nandhikeswara (Siva Abirami) was in the mix as well, having at it. She seemed to be enjoying herself. We saw from the endless videos that circulated on social media after that Murugan had been brought in dancing, and no doubt he was taken back to the temple dancing as well. It was rather hard to figure out in this context where ritual ended and just a most massive after-party began–or whether the former was being used to sacralise and justify the latter. At any rate, being ourselves rather more interested in ritual than party, found ourselves at the fringes and decided to call it a night, with an apology to Murugan who had a long night ahead of him yet, and a marriage to get to in the morning.

notes.title: Three Family Weddings in a Single Morning
body: The day after sashti is the day for the Murugan Thirukalyanam, because after the defeat of Soorapadman, Indra regains his kingdom. In gratitude, he offers his daughter Deivayanai (Devasena) in marriage to Murugan. We’re not sure why the Valli Kalyanam happens on this day, and speculate that the Murugan Thirukalyanam that also takes place at Panguni Utthiram is when that second wedding celebration happens. But we’re going to have to wait and see if that’s in fact the case. In the meantime, Valli isn’t excluded from today’s event. Murugan may be wedding Deivayanai, but he’s also wedded to Valli.

Three weddings happen this morning, at three temples, all in the hours between 9am and 11am. We find ourselves darting between Sundara Vinayaka, where Rami mam’s sister is the sponsor, and there’s the usual gathering of ladies there though a priest has been called in to do the homam and perform the nuptials. On one of our dartings, we find the women about to recite the whole of the Kanda Sashti Kavacham, which in a chorus sounds rather good. The temple has a mic set up, and speakers to broadcast beyond its four walls.
Nandhikeswara’s published schedule is below. Here, too, we dart in and out, but spend most time here as it’s just always a nice place to be.
7:00 AM: Maha Abhishekam (sacred bath) will be performed for Sri Gnana Velayudha Swami, accompanied by his consorts Sri Valli and Sri Devasena.

9:30 AM and 11:30 AM—during the Thiruvonam star and Thula Lagna—the divine wedding ceremony of Sri Gnana Velayudha Swami (with Sri Valli and Sri Devasena)—who resides and bestows his grace at the temple of Sri Nandi Emperuman—will take place.
Wedding Ceremony Schedule:

9:30 AM – Seeking the blessings (Anukkai) of Sri Gangai Vinayaka, followed by a ceremonial procession with offerings (Varisai Thattu) to the Yagasala (sacrificial hall, which is set up in the maha mandapa facing east).
10:00 AM – Thiruvilakku (lamp) worship, Varuna Kalasa puja, Maha Sankalpam (solemn vow/intention), and the chanting of the Kandar Kalivenba (from the Thirumurai scriptures).

This will be followed by the tying of the Mangala Naan (sacred wedding necklace) upon Sri Valli and Sri Devasena, along with Maha Shodasha Raja Upacharas (sixteen grand royal offerings), the recitation of Pancha Puranam and Thiruppugazh, and hymns of praise.

Ghousiga Balasubramania Swami’s Thirukalyanam of course was the biggest affair of the morning. A stage had been set up blocking the road, and the entire length of road up to the temple entrance was packed with people. Two large groups of women were seated in two large enclosures that had been demarcated, one behind the other, directly in front of the stage. A third enclosure was standing room only. The road was dense with bodies, no way to cut through if you came in from the wrong entrance. The temple itself had a long queue as well. We got there after going to Sundara Vinayaka and Nandhikeswara, and had little hope of any but the most distant views. The wedding itself was just coming to a conclusion anyway, so we got just a few atmospheric photos and left – beat it out of there, more like it. I admire the patience of those who sit and wait long for “swami darshan,” but the endless stream of beautifully dressed women and people from just about all the other temples we know was a little bewildering. There are other Thirukalyanams happening in the area, after all, and some with less hype and more space than Ghousiga–what is pulling everyone here?

Janardhanan (the man who comes to play the drums for Kailaya vadyam, and to carry the deities sometimes) had told us that Ghousiga was “the most trending” place to be. We’ve seen the priests at work and do not doubt either capacity or sincerity, but the place does indeed have a trending party-show atmosphere that gives a whole new sort of meaning to what John Zavos and I, in our introduction to the special issue of the International Journal of Hindu Studies [2009, 13(3): 241-260] once called “show temples.”  At the time, we recorded the objection of some folks from the BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha: “show temples,” they suggested, “implied that the principle purpose of modern temple building was an outward expression of the power of particular organisations; rather, they argued, the building of such temples was an inward-looking act of devotion, part of a broader approach based on selfless service, or seva, which was central to their understanding of themselves as Hindus” (2009: 243). But it’s time now for a rethink on this one. Ghousiga has none of the grandeur or global ambitions of BAPS’ projects. The people there are kind, know their regulars by name and face, are always responsive when approached, and genuinely human in their bearing. But the temple sure does take pains to put on / make space for some mighty big shows, to court social media popularity, and to invite attention. And so a temple with the thinnest “marabinar” (community traditions, heritage) as one of the elderly men in the Lawspet Murugan Koyil put it, could get so popular, the streets were no longer enough to contain its crowds.

So this was a morning of family weddings: all three temples we saw belong to individual families, as it happens. Two were modest, in proportion to size and means. But the hype and hoopla all belonged to Ghousiga.

notes.title: The Sheer Fun of the Old India
body: The morning at Lawspet was a panchamurti abhishekam which we couldn’t make it to with all the weddings happening in town, but it happened there late (we were told) and the dhvajavarohanam also happened. One of the gurukkals told us to save our energies for the evening, which we rather gladly did.

In the evening, Valli and Devasena (or Devayanai, Devyani), were taken to a house in a nearby street–where the family of Murugan arrived to “see the girl” (ponnu pakkaradu). Having seen and apparently liked them both, the procession carried the brides both back to the temple, coming around the madaveethi as usual. Arun followed them all the way, I met them near the small Vinayaka koyil on the main road where the Samharam had taken place. All the ladies accompanied as is the custom, and they had enlisted all the younger girls, including some very cute looking very young ones to help out. They all stood holding plates and trays filled with fruits and sweet things, weighted according to carrying capacity, the little ones especially looking so pleased to be included and their participation so sought. It was a lovely sight to behold. They waited outside the temple, brides behind them, until the priest’s wife, herself with an infant on her hip, did an arati, poured the red water under the pallakku being borne, and then everyone entered the temple. They went left to the back where the homa kunda and other prep for the wedding was set up. There was barely moving room anywhere in the temple. Many had sat for long holding their spots. Lucky for us, we happened to the right spot, just near the nadaswaram players. On the right end were the brides, on the left Murugan arrived–grandly, as all grooms must.

I had not fully anticipated the fun that would now ensue. Most other thirukalyanams do some flower tossing and garland exchanging and the like. But these can be formal and not lively – here they were practically a show.

Three priests had the parivattam tied on their heads, including Venkatesa gurukkal, who asked me to guess his age, he’s 78! And feeling the weight of ageing, but not showing it for a minute. He danced! He swayed with the malas, and got on all fours and then on 2s to become a snake (to the tune of aadu paambe–why is this such a favourite at these events? Ghousiga made much of this sequence as well in their dances). Together the priests all three were such sports, and such fun entertainment. The men carrying Murugan lowered him as he swooned to the mesmerising tune and snake-head movements–they danced, too, all evening long–Venkatesa gurukkal used his hands to strike and sting the other priests more than a few times. Whoever thought these ritual specialists needed also to be performers and dancers? But they do, and how they rose to the occasion. The women around me directed my gaze to this or that to get the right photos. Everyone was jovial and accommodating and just happy, as folks should be at a wedding like this one.

We left when the brides joined their groom to enter the mandapam, figuring it would be pro forma from here. But this was a brilliant build-up. Who says Ghousiga Balasubramanian has the corner on dance? The crowd at Lawspet came from the neighbouring community, not from far-flung places, not so much lured by Insta-fame or “trending” anything, but by the temple that holds this neighbourhood still. They do their share of instagram posting, drones flew and screens broadcast and cameras were plenty beyond just us. But what drew people was still something much more palpably local, rooted in the proudly Sengunthar Mudaliar traditions of this place, and that was just so very nice. The old India, the best of it.

What we missed this evening, having given ourselves to Lawspet: the Vedapuriswara Thirukalyana utsavam–but we noted that it happened (followed by manjaneer on the 17th, unjal on the 18th, vidaiyatri on the 19th and finally utsava shanti on the 20th, practically mirroring the schedule at Lawspet). Chetty Koyil also had a wedding (unsure of time) and an unjal utsavam on the 17th.

notes.title: Manjal Neer Utsavam
body: The month Karthikai began today, and Lawspet Murugan Koyil celebrated this with the Manjal Neer Utsavam. Although called an utsavam, it seems to exist today as a far more diminished event. We reached around 730pm and found the usual pre-purappadu aradhanai going on for the utsava murtis. At the end of this, apart from the two regular elderly odhuvars, song was offered by a young girl who seemed to be the ubhayakara’s daughter. Upon completion she was given reassuring smiles by the priests and elders. This was followed by an elaborate vadyam offering made by three nadaswaram and two thavil players. They played three ragas as Sriram Gurukkal announced them. One of them was the Aadu Pambe tune also played for the Thirukalyanam on the night before, which seems a real performer’s favourite at temple events – though now that we did not have the dancing priests to grab all our attention (!!) we could focus a little on the winding serpentine inflections of the song.

With the music session then wrapped up, the purappadu began. One round of the prakaram, then out onto the streets. We were a little confused about the ‘Manjal Neer-ness’ of this all, and upon enquiry found that that was a small event before the aradhanai where manjal-water was sprinkled on the deities and devotees. So not much of an utsavam, but something nonetheless, perhaps remnant of a grander past existence which may have given it its name.

notes.title: Back to Lonely Nights and Long Trails
body: “The dancing after sashti will be 50% reduced,” one of the nadaswaram players had once remarked. We missed the send-off from Ghousiga, but found Murugan with Vinayaka and Veerabahu on Bharati street about to come into the market area. Were there nadaswaram players leading the way? Somehow neither of us could recall hearing their heralding sounds. The little red Ghousiga tractor was leading the way. It’s funny, but Ghousiga’s temple crowd seems so entirely different from their madaveethi crowd, comprised of what households remain on their path, what temples are open when they pass, and all the market women who don’t look like those we’ve ever seen at the temple itself, but who stop the procession unfailingly and offer Rs 10, Rs 20, whatever they pull out of their sari knots doubling as money belts. This isn’t the Insta crew. The young priest who helps out recognised us and gave us extra flowers. He’d also been the one to tell us that the deity who comes out in the mornings is the pradhana murti who was there from the beginning. The evening purappadu takes out the samhara murti, only recently acquired.
